certificates.intro: iOS and Android reject self-signed certificates, like the one Portainer generates by default on port 9443. The app can't override this: the fix is to present the device with a certificate it trusts. Here are three ways to get there, from the simplest to the most hands-on.

tailscale.title: Tailscale
tailscale.bestFor: Best for reaching your server from anywhere, without opening a port.
tailscale.summary: Tailscale provides a valid Let's Encrypt certificate for your server's address on your Tailscale network.
steps: Install Tailscale on the server and on this phone, on the same network.
In the Tailscale admin console, enable MagicDNS and HTTPS certificates (DNS tab).
On the server, serve Portainer over HTTPS:
Sign in with the machine's address on your Tailscale network:
tailscale.note: "https+insecure" only covers the local hop between Tailscale and Portainer, on the server itself: this phone still gets a valid certificate.

reverse-proxy.title: Reverse proxy and Let's Encrypt
reverse-proxy.bestFor: Best if you already own a domain name.
reverse-proxy.summary: A reverse proxy obtains a Let's Encrypt certificate and presents it in place of Portainer's.
steps: Point a name, for example portainer.example.com, at your reverse proxy.
Put Portainer behind the proxy. With Caddy, on the same Docker network as the portainer container:
For a name only reachable on your local network, use Let's Encrypt's DNS challenge: Caddy, Traefik and Nginx Proxy Manager support it with most DNS providers.
Sign in with the proxy's address:

own-ca.title: Your own authority with mkcert
own-ca.bestFor: Best for a local network, without a domain name.
own-ca.summary: You create your own certificate authority, sign Portainer's certificate with it, then install that authority on this phone.
steps: On a computer, install mkcert, then create a certificate for the addresses you type in the app (name, IP, or both):
Start Portainer with this certificate, placed in a certs folder mounted on /certs:
Get the authority: it's the rootCA.pem file in the folder this command prints.
Send rootCA.pem to this phone (AirDrop, email, file), then install it as shown below.
own-ca.note: Never share rootCA-key.pem: anyone holding this key can create certificates this phone will accept, for any website.

certificates.deviceTrustTitle: Install the authority on this phone

ios: Open rootCA.pem on the iPhone: iOS offers to download a profile.
Settings › General › VPN & Device Management: install the profile.
Settings › General › About › Certificate Trust Settings: turn on full trust for this certificate. Without this step, iOS installs the profile but still refuses the connection.
android: Copy rootCA.pem to the phone. Rename it to rootCA.crt if the system doesn't offer to install it.
Settings › Security › Encryption & credentials › Install a certificate › CA certificate. The path varies by manufacturer: search the settings for "certificate".
Many apps ignore authorities installed this way. StackPilot does not: it accepts them just like the system ones.

certificates.footnote: Why not just accept Portainer's default certificate? The app would have to bypass the system's verification, which it doesn't do: the solutions above genuinely protect the connection, with no exception to manage.
